## Claims

### C-R1-01 | Hebrew title names key figure, not author
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** In the HB, 1–2 Samuel stand among the Former Prophets; the Hebrew title “Samuel” most likely names Samuel as the key figure who established monarchy by anointing Saul then David (the king-maker), not as author of the whole.
- **Quote:** "the Hebrew title “Samuel” most likely refers to Samuel not as the author, but as the key figure, the one who established the monarchy"
- **Locus:** [Page 2]; §I Title
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-02 | LXX/Vulgate title tradition (Books of Kingdoms)
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** LXX divides Samuel and Kings into four “Books of Kingdoms” (*basileiōn* A–D); Vulgate accordingly has 1–2 Kings for 1–2 Samuel.
- **Quote:** "the Septuagint (LXX), divides Samuel and Kings into the four “Books of Kingdoms” (basileiōn A-D)"
- **Locus:** [Page 2]; §I Title
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-03 | MT of Samuel is textually poor; multiple witnesses exist
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Besides MT (10th–11th c. MSS), 4QSama/b/c and versions (LXXB/A/L, OL, Targ. Jonathan, Syr., Vulg.; Josephus Ant.) matter for Samuel’s textual history; MT has suffered transcriptional corruption and is “in extremely poor condition.”
- **Quote:** "The MT of 1–2 Samuel has suffered from transcriptional corruption and is “in extremely poor condition”"
- **Locus:** [Pages 2–3]; §II Text
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-04 | Pre-Qumran eclectic correction of MT via LXX
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Thenius (1842) systematically used LXX to recover “original readings”; Wellhausen produced an “outline of an eclectic text”; Driver attended more to Hebrew grammar/syntax; de Boer was wholly negative toward correcting MT by LXX.
- **Quote:** "the first systematic attempt at correction was made by Otto Thenius… who used the LXX to recover the “original readings”"
- **Locus:** [Pages 3–4]; §II.A.1 Before DSS
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-05 | Qumran Samuel scrolls closer to LXX tradition
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** 4QSama (50–25 B.C., large, much of 1–2 Sam), 4QSamb (mid-3rd c. B.C., fragments of 1 Sam 16/19/21/23; possibly oldest biblical MS at Qumran), 4QSamc (early 1st c. B.C., small fragments) diverge widely from MT and, per Cross, are consistently close to the Hebrew reflected by LXX—so LXX may reflect a different MS tradition.
- **Quote:** "These biblical scroll and fragments diverge widely from the MT and, according to Cross, are consistently close to the one reflected by LXX."
- **Locus:** [Pages 4–5]; §II.A.2 Discovery of Qumran
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-06 | Cross’s local texts theory doubted
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Cross proposes a “local texts theory”: Palestinian (Qumran-like), Babylonian (MT), Egyptian (OG in LXXB); recent studies (Aejmelaeus, Saiz, Herbert) cast significant doubt on a proto-Lucianic recension based on a 4QSama-like text.
- **Quote:** "recent studies by Aejmalaeus, Saiz, and Herbert certainly cast significant doubt on Cross’s theory"
- **Locus:** [Pages 5–6]; §II.A.3 Local Texts Theory
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-07 | Eclectic reconstruction of Samuel is weakly grounded
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** McCarter reconstructs eclectically (MT tends to skip; Qumran-type to expand); objections include insufficient witnesses (unlike NT), decisions ad sensum (Walters), and only 4QSama being securely a “biblical text” (other two may be paraphrases).
- **Quote:** "unlike the case of the NT, there are not enough manuscript witnesses to reconstruct a primitive text of Samuel."
- **Locus:** [Page 6]; §II.A.4 Conventional Textual Criticism
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-08 | Single original vs multiple pristine texts; Tsumura’s stance
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Tov summarizes two theories: single original text (majority: McCarter, Tov, R. Klein, Stoebe) vs different pristine texts (Kahle, Barthélemy, Goshen-Gottstein, Talmon, Greenberg, Walters). Tsumura holds one available reading could be nearer the original and does not give up approaching a more original text, while avoiding hasty generalizations.
- **Quote:** "the present writer holds that one of the available readings could be nearer to the original than the others."
- **Locus:** [Pages 6–7]; §II.A.4
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-09 | LXX limitations; lectio difficilior; 1 Sam 1:24 pārîm
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** LXX is a translation, itself corruptible; where LXX is clear and MT hard, translators often guessed from an MT-like text. Emending 1 Sam 1:24 *pārîm šelōšāh* (“three bulls”) to “a three-year-old bull” via LXX/4QSama/Peshitta is wrong if *pārîm* has older sense “younglings”—primary task is interpret data in context, not alter data.
- **Quote:** "Going to the LXX is often against the principle of lectio difficilior… the animals which Hannah brought to Shiloh were not necessarily adult “bulls,” but the “younglings”"
- **Locus:** [Pages 7–8]; §II.B.2 LXX’s Limitations; on 1 Sam 1:24
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[shiloh]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-10 | Higher regard for MT; phonetic spellings not scribal errors
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Overemphasis on LXX vs MT has been criticized (Barthélemy, Pisano et al.); recent trend (BHQ) values Masoretic tradition more. Many proposed “scribal errors” may be phonetic spellings or misunderstood grammar; aural features of narrative matter.
- **Quote:** "many of the “scribal errors” in 1–2 Samuel suggested by textual critics may be in fact phonetic spellings or Hebrew grammatical constructions that have been misunderstood."
- **Locus:** [Pages 8–10]; §II.B.3–4
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-11 | Phonology exemplars: 2 Sam 22:40 wattazrēnî; 1 Sam 15:9 nemibzāh
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** MT *wattazrēnî* (2 Sam 22:40) can be sandhi from *watte’azzerēnî* (loss of intervocalic aleph → vowel sandhi → shorter form), not defective; *nemibzāh* (1 Sam 15:9) can be Ni. ptc. f.s. of *bzh* with m-glide and restructuring, reflecting pronunciation not error.
- **Quote:** "there is no need to reckon the MT Samuel here as textually defective."
- **Locus:** [Pages 9–10]; §II.B.4 Scribal Errors or Phonetic Spellings?
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-12 | Brachylogy vs haplography: 1 Sam 14:42 happîlû
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** In 1 Sam 14:42 *happîlû* (“decide,” lit. “cause to fall”) lacks object; McCarter’s long-haplography solution misses brachylogy—ellipsis of “lots” in the idiom *npl* (Hi.) + *gôrāl*; verb alone retains idiomatic sense “to decide.”
- **Quote:** "Such “text-critical” solutions miss the characteristics of linguistic phenomenon such as brachylogy"
- **Locus:** [Page 10]; §II.B.5 Idiomatic Expressions; also [Page 64–65] §VII.D
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-13 | Prefer unaltered MT; majority of emendations needless
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Without solid evidence of corruption, leave MT unaltered with minimal speculation; some passages still seem unintelligible (13:21; 17:12) or strange (9:24; 13:1, 8; 20:14), but Tsumura holds majority of proposed emendations needless.
- **Quote:** "the present author feels he has shown that the majority of proposed emendations are needless."
- **Locus:** [Page 10]; §II.B.5 close
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-14 | Authorship unknown; staged composition; final edit ≤ late 10th c.
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Author of Samuel unknown; name not authorship (Samuel dies 1 Sam 25:1; 28:3). Composition/editing in stages: Ark story (1 Sam 4:1–7:1) possibly pre-Davidic; Saul-and-David (1 Sam 16–31) earliest early Davidic Jerusalem; Story of King David (2 Sam 1–20) later Davidic or Solomonic; final editing with minor adjustments probably no later than late 10th c. B.C. (1 Sam 27:6 “Ziklag… to this day”).
- **Quote:** "The final editing of 1–2 Samuel, with minor adjustments, was probably made no later than the late 10th century B.C."
- **Locus:** [Page 11]; §III Date and Authorship intro
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[david]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-15 | Three putative sources (AN, HDR, SN/CH) — existence as independent works doubted
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Earlier critics posited J/E (pro-/anti-monarchic) strata (overemphasized; J/E existence suspect); Gressmann fragmentary hypothesis and Rost’s composite materials remain influential. Widely held three major pre-final compositions: Ark Narrative, History of David’s Rise, Succession Narrative/Court History—but whether these “blocks” ever existed as single works is still in doubt.
- **Quote:** "whether these “blocks” ever existed as single works is still in doubt."
- **Locus:** [Pages 11–12]; §III.A Three Putative Sources
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[monarchy-request]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-16 | Ark Narrative not proven independent; early vs Davidic strata
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Rost’s AN (1 Sam 4:1b–7:1 + parts of 2 Sam 6) is hard to prove as one original story: vocabulary/style similarity not decisive (Miller/Roberts); Kiriath-jearim vs Baalah of Judah; in 2 Sam 6 David, not Yahweh/ark, takes initiative. 1 Sam 4–6 likely among oldest (no royal Jerusalem cult); possibly contemporary with Samuel, while 2 Sam 6 is early Davidic. Story of Ark (4:1–7:1) is embedded in Story of Samuel (1:1–7:17); AN as independent composition unproven.
- **Quote:** "it has still not been proved that the AN as such ever existed as an independent composition."
- **Locus:** [Pages 12–13]; §III.A.1 Ark Narrative
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-17 | HDR reframed as “Story of Saul and David” (1 Sam 16–31)
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Scholars posit independent HDR (1 Sam 15/16–2 Sam 5/7) to legitimize David; McCarter dates earliest versions to David’s reign via Hattušiliš parallel. Tsumura prefers 1 Sam 16–31 as literary unit “Story of Saul and David,” linked to “Story of King David” (2 Sam 1–20) via 2 Sam 1 (A/aB transitional technique). Positing independent HDR may do “palpable violence to the beautiful integrity of the story” (Alter); Dietrich/Naumann support HDR never existed as single work.
- **Quote:** "this author would take 1 Samuel 16–31, rather than 1 Samuel 15/16-2 Samuel 5/-7, as a literary unit… the “Story of Saul and David”"
- **Locus:** [Pages 13–14]; §III.A.2 History of David’s Rise
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[saul]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-18 | SN vs Court History; epilogues not mere appendices
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Rost’s SN (2 Sam 9–20 + 1 Kgs 1–2) as pro-Solomonic eyewitness propaganda is contested (Eissfeldt CH; Gunn novel/entertainment; Ackerman freedom/divine sovereignty; Alter questions succession as central concern). Chs. 21–24 are better “epilogues” (structurally integral) than “appendices” (later additions); Araunah’s threshing floor prepares for Solomon’s temple. Prefer 2 Sam 1–20 as unified “Story of King David.”
- **Quote:** "generally speaking, while an “appendix” implies a later addition to the main part, an “epilogue” constitutes a structurally integral part of the entire story."
- **Locus:** [Pages 14–16]; §III.A.3 Succession Narrative / Court History?
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-19 | Noth’s DH; Tsumura’s skepticism of late Deuteronomistic redaction language
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Noth’s Dtr compiled Joshua–Kings; for Samuel, Noth limited Dtr contributions to 1 Sam 7–8, 12, part of 10, 2 Sam 5:6–12, and chronological notes. Cross’s two editions (Josianic + Exilic ~550) and multi-stage theories rest on questionable linguistic assumptions: “to this day,” “abandon Yahweh / serve other gods,” *ntn byd* etc. are not automatically late Deuteronomistic—parallels in earlier OT and ANE (incl. Amarna *ntn byd*; Akk. “until now”). Circular reasoning: late norms project onto earlier-looking passages.
- **Quote:** "the conventional theories of “redaction” rest on questionable assumptions concerning the nature of language… Much of the reasoning seems circular."
- **Locus:** [Pages 16–19]; §III.B.1 Noth’s Hypothesis
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[covenant]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-20 | 1 Sam 27:6 as terminus ante quem for final editing
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** “Therefore Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day” (1 Sam 27:6) seems early Divided Monarchy, probably early Rehoboam, not later than late 10th c.—after Shishak’s campaign (925 B.C.) the city would not have belonged to Judah. By contrast 1 Sam 6:18b “until this day” for Abel platform likely pre-Davidic (ark moved to Jerusalem under David).
- **Quote:** "1 Sam. 27:6… seems to have been written early in the Divided Monarchy, probably during the early days of Rehoboam’s era, not later than the late 10th century B.C."
- **Locus:** [Pages 17–18]; §III.B.1
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-21 | Holistic literary approaches and post-modernism assessed
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Late 20th-c. shift from historical-critical isolation of units to final-form literary-rhetorical study (Gunn, Jobling, Fokkelman, Sternberg, Eslinger, Alter); structuralist priority of synchrony. Post-modern/deconstruction/intertextuality (Miscall, Derrida, Lyke) sidelining authorial intent is inadequate for biblical hermeneutics—need competence in original ANE cultural-historical settings. Literary approach useful without pre-history hypotheses, but linguistic analysis in context must come first.
- **Quote:** "for the Hebrew text… it is only when one has first analyzed it linguistically in its immediate context and learned as much as possible about the historical background that one can appreciate the content of the story properly."
- **Locus:** [Pages 19–23]; §III.B.2 Holistic Literary Approaches
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-22 | Historiography vs historicity; maximalist vs minimalist
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Shift from historicity to historiography (Brettler) has sometimes marginalized biblical texts (Provan critiquing Whitelam/Thompson). Minimalists deny biblical claims without extra-biblical proof—including United Kingdom monarchy, even Josianic reform/Jehu/Shishak despite evidence. Tsumura endorses Hallo’s maximalism: use every scrap of evidence; ANE comparative/contextual approach (Gordon, Kitchen, Hallo) illuminates rather than merely “proves.” Principle: “The absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.” Religious reference does not make biblical narrative unhistorical (cf. Assyrian, Mesha, Zakir inscriptions).
- **Quote:** "Hallo is a “maximalist” because he says “the historian of antiquity has no alternative but to use every scrap of evidence available.”"
- **Locus:** [Pages 23–29]; §III.C Historiography
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-23 | Extra-biblical David: Tel Dan, possibly Mesha, Shoshenq
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Tel Dan late 9th-c. *bytdwd* most probably “House of David” (against Davies et al.)—first attestation of name David; Lemaire’s Mesha reading *b(y)t-[d]wd* may be another 9th-c. reference; Kitchen notes possible “highland/heights of David” in Shoshenq I list (ca. 924 B.C.), “barely 50 years after his death.”
- **Quote:** "for the first time the name “David” has been attested."

### C-R1-24 | ANE analogies allow early “eternal dynasty” and early phraseology
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Redaction critics often call 2 Sam 7 “eternal dynasty” postexilic; Laato: early Assyrian royal building inscriptions near David’s time show such concept possible already when David planned a temple. Millard: Assyrian royal inscriptions reuse style over centuries—so “Deuteronomistic” phrases in late texts do not force late dating of all texts with similar phrases. Running records/diaries on wax tablets (lūaḥ) possible Hebrew parallel.
- **Quote:** "it seems mistaken to claim that just because certain “Deuteronomistic” phrases appear in undeniably late Hebrew texts, any text containing these phrases must have been written about the same time."

### C-R1-25 | Early linguistic data argue against postexilic redaction
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Archaic/early terms understood via Ugaritic/Akkadian but later obscure argue early writing: *ḥămôr leḥem* (1 Sam 16:20) as calque of Akk. *imēru* “ass-measure,” not omer/homer; *ṣemed* (1 Sam 14:14) as Akk. *ṣimdu* area measure; *pār* “youngling” (1:24); *na‘ar* “young/offspring” (2:13); *sēper* for “letter” not LBH *’iggeret* (2 Sam 11:14). A postexilic redactor would modernize obsolete measurement terms; retention suggests early-monarchic editorial perspective.
- **Quote:** "These early words suggest that the author was writing in an early period, much earlier than exilic or postexilic times."
- **Locus:** [Pages 29–31]; §III.C.5 Linguistic Data and Dating

### C-R1-26 | Tentative compositional history (United Monarchy → late 10th c. final edit)
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Tentatively: Story of Samuel (1–7), ch. 8 (monarchy intro), Story of Saul (9–15), Story of Saul and David (16–31), Story of King David (2 Sam 1–20), Epilogues (21–24) existed under United Monarchy before unified edit. Possible dating of parts: Samuel + Ark + “Right of the King” early Samuel’s ministry; Story of Saul later Samuel era; Saul-and-David early David (justify kingship vs Saulides); King David late David/early Solomon (Halpern: acquit David of serial murder). Final editors: minimal framing (Alter); combine existing stories + Epilogues; ~ late 10th c. / early Rehoboam (27:6). View remains hypothetical. Hebrew historiography need not wait for 7th-c./postexilic Dtr (Gressmann; Gordon via Gilboa/Aqhat).
- **Quote:** "They probably worked around a time not later than the late 10th century, that is, the early period of Rehoboam’s reign, in light of the comment… 1 Sam. 27:6."
- **Locus:** [Pages 31–32]; §III.C.6 Tentative Conclusions

### C-R1-27 | Early Iron Age / Philistine historical frame
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Samuel’s background is Early Iron Age ca. 1200–1000 B.C.: transition from LB empires to small kingdoms; Sea Peoples/Philistines settle southern Palestine ca. 1200; iron technology spreads; Philistines likely adopt Canaanite language and possibly standardized Phoenician alphabet. Transitional Israelite polity: Eli→Samuel→Saul→David; Saul’s kingdom more than loose confederation but not yet strong central rule.
- **Quote:** "The books of Samuel deal with a transitional period in the history of ancient Israel — the transition, first, from the priest Eli to the judge Samuel, then from the judge Samuel to the king Saul, then from Saul to David"
- **Locus:** [Pages 33–34]; §IV Historical and Religious Background intro + A
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[david]], [[philistines]], [[israelites]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-28 | Philistine pentapolis, garrisons, iron monopoly, relations with Samuel/Saul/David
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Philistines form pentapolis (Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon; then Gath, Ekron); aim to control routes via posts/garrisons; major victory mid-11th c. under Eli (1 Sam 4); Samuel victory near Mizpah (7:7–11); under Saul garrisons, *mašḥit*, economic subjugation via iron metallurgy monopoly (13:19–21); David breaks Philistine power (captures Dor, Megiddo, Beth-shean) though not major southern coastal cities; uses Cherethite/Pelethite/Gittite mercenaries. Philistines “uncircumcised” but highly developed technologically/culturally.
- **Quote:** "Those Philistines were certainly “uncircumcised,” but they were not the uncultivated and unsophisticated people that medieval Europe once thought them to be."
- **Locus:** [Pages 34–37]; §IV.B Israel and the Philistines
- **Targets:** [[philistines]], [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[david]], [[israelites]], [[1-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-29 | Canaanite religion background (Ugarit/Emar); no Israelite royal deification
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Canaanite religion illuminates Samuel; Ugaritic/Emar LB evidence used cautiously for Iron Age practices. Ugaritic pantheon: *ilib* (divine ancestor) top—ancestor cult importance; *rpum*/*mlkm*; *marzēaḥ*; Dagan (3rd; Philistines adopt as national deity); Baal (fertility/storm; temptation, 1 Sam 7:4; 12:10 with Astarte); solar cult (*špš*). In biblical religion kings not divine; no postmortem deification of David/Abraham/Samuel; no *marzēaḥ* for Samuel’s burial (25:1).
- **Quote:** "There is no practice of postmortem deification in 1–2 Samuel. Even King David and great figures such as Abraham and Samuel were not deified after death."
- **Locus:** [Pages 38–41]; §IV.C Canaan and Canaanites

### C-R1-30 | Necromancy / spirits of the dead; Endor; OT prohibitions
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Popular necromancy: Endor’s *’ĕlōhîm* (28:13) as spirits of the dead / preternatural beings (// Ugar. *rpim–ilnym*, *ilm–mtm*); Isa 8:19; Ps 106:28 // Num 25:2. Endor is necromancy not ancestor worship; Saul banished mediums (28:3); OT forbids mediums/necromancers/offerings to dead/self-laceration (Deut 18:11 etc.). Persistence of “pagan” cults despite prohibition; Endor shows futility (announcement of death) yet something unusual by God’s power beyond necromancer’s control. Yahweh alone holds authority over life/death (Hannah: 1 Sam 2:6).
- **Quote:** "The story of the “Witch of Endor” teaches us how futile it is to call upon the practice of necromancy, since conjuring the dead resulted in an announcement of death for Saul."

### C-R1-31 | Royal cult contrast: Saul New Moon vs Ugaritic sacral kingship
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Saul presides over New Moon festival meal as royal family head (1 Sam 20:5) with no indication of priestly role; Ugaritic kings play sacral role in monthly royal dynastic rituals, sacrificing to *ilib* and deities for ancestral blessings. ### C-R1-32 | Grammar: unusual topicalization with wayhî / topic before waw+V
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Before reconstructing history/theology, grasp linguistic peculiarities; some “impossible” forms may be forgotten constructions. - **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-33 | Relative clause insertion; speaker-oriented kî
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Relative clause inserted into main clause can make adverbial phrase seem part of relative clause when it belongs to main (2 Sam 11:27 clear; 1 Sam 26:3 by geography). Speaker-oriented *kî* (“reason I said [A] is [B]”) vs causal *kî*; 1 Sam 2:1 *kî* not prosaic addition but reason for three performative utterances.
- **Quote:** "By understanding the “speaker-oriented” ki we can understand the structure of narrative discourses such as those in 1–2 Samuel better than before."
- **Locus:** [Pages 48–49]; §V.B–C
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-34 | Discourse analysis method: SETTING–EVENT–TERMINUS; wayqtl ranks
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Discourse analysis (beyond sentence) is necessary for Samuel narratives; limited by lost prosody. Hopper foreground/background; Longacre 1989 Joseph story milestone—main line = verb-initial *wayqtl*s. Tsumura applies thoroughly (claims first commentary to do so for Samuel). Episode structure: SETTING–EVENT–TERMINUS–(TRANSITION); EVENT begins with *wayqtl* + stated subject; “initial” vs “sequential” waw; verb-rank system with “principle of relativity.” *wayqtl* of motion/stative verbs often SETTING not EVENT; impersonal/3 m.p. without subject often TERMINUS/TRANSITION. Worked example: 1 Sam 18:5.
- **Quote:** "no commentary has appeared which applies this analysis thoroughly to the Hebrew text of 1–2 Samuel. Since the present volume pursues such an analysis"
- **Locus:** [Pages 49–52]; §VI Discourse Analysis A
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-35 | Transitional techniques / links (Parunak); tempo; viewpoint
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Parunak “transitional techniques”: patterns A/aB, Ab/B, Ab/aB, A/ab/B (hinge). Ex.: 1 Sam 3:1 links to ch. 2 via “boy… ministering” (A/aB); 2 Sam 1 as “a” of A/aB between 1 Sam and 2 Sam 2–20. Tempo: Goliath’s repeated “the Philistine” (17:41–44) vs David’s rapid 14 *wayqtl*s (17:48–51); parenthetical slowdowns (2 Sam 13:18a; 1 Sam 7:10f.). Viewpoint via “come/go”: “take and go” vs “take and come”; 2 Sam 19:25 *bā’ yerûšālaim* preferred as “came from Jerusalem” (viewpoint near Jordan). Samuel is primarily “aural” text.
- **Quote:** "the Hebrew narrative, which is primarily an “aural” text (i.e., one that is to be heard) and written as if it were to be read aloud."
- **Locus:** [Pages 53–55]; §VI.B–D
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[philistines]], [[jonathan]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-36 | Vertical grammar of parallelism; poetic prose
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Parallelism = “one through two lines”; vertical grammar—dependency across lines (ellipsis of verb/subject; split phrases). Examples: 1 Sam 2:10b king//anointed; 2:4 chiastic bow/feeble; 2 Sam 22:15, 42. “Vertical grammar” also in prose narrative (e.g. 1 Sam 2:14 “at Shiloh” modifies “was done” vertically, ax//x′b—not McCarter’s emendation of *šām*; 1 Sam 28:19 as tricolon not conflation). Poetic features widely in Samuel narrative; aural text invites detection.
- **Quote:** "the grammar of poetic parallelism is characterized by “vertical grammar,” in which the elements of lines have grammatical dependency on each other “vertically” as well as “horizontally.”"
- **Locus:** [Pages 55–60]; §VII.A–B
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[shiloh]], [[saul]], [[philistines]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-37 | AXB literary insertion pattern
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** AXB = rhetorical insertion of grammatically/semantically different X into complex AB that normally stays together; A–B keep unity; X relates to AB as whole; slows tempo/suspense—not later redactional insertion. Realizations: broken construct chain, interrupted hendiadys/merismus, tricolon A//X//B, inserted bicolon A//x//y//B. Exx.: 1 Sam 2:2 (LXX-omitted X line as AXB not gloss); 2 Sam 3:33b–34a (interrupted “hands and feet”; qinah); 1 Sam 10:2 Rachel’s tomb AXB (not McCarter’s LXX-based emendation). Macro AXBY in 1 Sam 28–31 alternating David (A–B) and Saul (X–Y). Not mixture of literary sources but mono-dimensional linguistic description of multi-dimensional events.
- **Quote:** "This “insertion” of X is a rhetorical technique of an author, not a compositional one, which assumes that someone inserted an element into a text later."
- **Locus:** [Pages 60–64]; §VII.C Literary Insertion: AXB Pattern
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-38 | Brachylogy and idiom further exemplars
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Brachylogy = omission of key word in idiom. Object ellipsis: *krt* without *brt* “covenant” (1 Sam 22:8; 11:2; 20:16); *happîlû* without lots (14:42); also 2:5; 8:3; 12:6; 18:11; 20:42. Subject ellipsis: 1 Sam 24:11 “I pitied” = “(my eye) looked with compassion”—body terms often omitted; not accidental loss. Prefer style/grammar over assuming textual corruption.
- **Quote:** "Before treating the texts of 1–2 Samuel as “corrupt,” we ought to read the them according to their own style and grammar"
- **Locus:** [Pages 64–65]; §VII.D Brachylogy and Idiom
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[covenant]], [[jonathan]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-39 | Four-block literary structure of 1 Samuel + 2 Samuel frame
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** 1 Samuel = three major stories + transitional monarchy chapter: (I) Story of Samuel with embedded Ark (1:1–7:17: rise 1–3; Ark 4:1–7:1; judgeship 7:2–17); (II) transition “Appoint us a king” (8:1–22); (III) Story of Saul (9:1–15:35: made king 9–11; Samuel’s address 12; reign 13–15); (IV) Story of Saul and David (16:1–31:13) with detailed substructure. Plus (V) Story of King David 2 Sam 1–20; (VI) Epilogues 2 Sam 21–24. Overall delimited by poems: Hannah’s Song (1 Sam 2) and David’s Song/Last Words (2 Sam 22–23) as inclusio; 2 Sam 1 as transitional A/aB link; 21–24 concentric ABCBA integral epilogues (not secondary Appendix); 1 Kgs 1–2 as A/aB link to Solomon story, possibly slightly later than late-10th-c. Samuel editors.
- **Quote:** "The First Book of Samuel is composed of three major stories… and a transitional section on the introduction of the monarchy (ch. 8)."
- **Locus:** [Pages 65–68]; §VIII.A Literary Structure of 1 Samuel
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[david]], [[jonathan]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[monarchy-request]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-40 | Hannah’s Song: three literary themes of 1–2 Samuel
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Song of Hannah (prototype of Magnificat Luke 1:46–55) is “thematic and structural introduction to Samuel” (Bailey). Built-in themes: (1) Yahweh’s holy sovereignty (vv. 1–3, 6–7, 8b–10a); (2) reversal of human fortunes (vv. 4–5, 8b); (3) kingship (v. 10b). Theme 2 developed here; 1 and 3 in Theology section; kingship more thoroughly in 2 Samuel intro.
- **Quote:** "the literary themes of the books 1–2 Samuel seem to be built into the Song of Hannah… (1) Yahweh’s holy sovereignty… (2) the reversal of human fortunes… and (3) the theme of kingship"
- **Locus:** [Pages 68–69]; §VIII.B Themes of 1 Samuel
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[david]], [[jonathan]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-41 | Reversal of fortune motif across main characters
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Hannah’s praise that “human fate is reversed by God’s will” plays out in Hannah, Samuel (boy vs Eli’s junior-priest sons; Eli’s house falls, Samuel rises), Saul (obscure clan → first king), David (youngest anointed over seven brothers; Jonathan acknowledges inferiority; Spirit from Saul to David). Divine presence with David (16:18) is leitmotiv of Story of Saul and David; *ḥesed* as unmerited favor (20:8, 14–15). Martin’s whole-Samuel reversal analysis partly forced.
- **Quote:** "The divine presence with David (see 1 Sam. 16:18) is the leitmotiv of the “Story of Saul and David.”"
- **Locus:** [Pages 68–69]; §VIII.B The Reversal of Human Fortune
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[david]], [[jonathan]], [[divine-providence]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-42 | Theology: kingship of God; human king as deputy only
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** God is King of Universe from eternity (Ps 29:10; Exod 15:18 premonarchic); no human king except as deputy of divine King (on 8:7). First “king” word in Samuel at 1 Sam 2:10—Hannah: Lord gives power to his human deputy and lifts horn of his anointed; Lord “judges the ends of the earth.” All humans “royal” as image of God (Gen) unlike ANE where only kings are deity’s image. When God allows a human king (8:6b–9), only as earthly vice-regent. Yahweh’s sovereignty over Israel and Philistines (7:13); not attained by victory over chaos (unlike Marduk/Baal). Title: “Lord of Hosts who sits on the cherubim” (4:4).
- **Quote:** "when God allowed the people of Israel to have a human king (1 Sam. 8:6b-9), he gave them a king only as God’s earthly vice-regent or deputy."
- **Locus:** [Pages 69–70]; §IX.A Kingship of God
- **Targets:** [[kingship-in-israel]], [[monarchy-request]], [[1-samuel]], [[covenant]], [[philistines]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-43 | Theology: providential guidance; ordinary life; Davidic covenant as turning point
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Rom 8:28 summarizes author’s intent: God providentially guides chosen individuals (Hannah, Samuel, David); even Saul under providential care (9:16) though rejected for disobedience (chs. 13, 15). Not “Fate”; perfect timing (chs. 9, 24). Saving plan in ordinary life (Peninnah hardship; donkey search → Samuel; food errand → Goliath). Later: David’s plea to build a house (2 Sam 7:5) becomes occasion for eternal dynasty promise (2 Sam 7:16)—turning point in outworking of saving purposes; Matt 1:1 places David mid genealogy of Messiah.
- **Quote:** "this promise to, or “covenant” with, David was the turning point in the outworking of God’s saving purposes."
- **Locus:** [Pages 70–71]; §IX.B God’s Providential Guidance
- **Targets:** [[divine-providence]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[covenant]], [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[david]], [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-44 | Theology: sovereign will, obedience, justice and mercy
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** God is “God of true knowledge” (2:3b); chooses/rejects by absolute sovereign will; “does not change his mind… not a man” (15:29) though dealings may change. Obedience prime: boy Samuel hears (ch. 3); Saul fails (13; 15); David fights for Yahweh’s name (17) then fails adultery/murder (2 Sam 11); Nathan gives David second chance (2 Sam 12), Saul refused repentance (1 Sam 15). Only grace upholds sinful humans before holy God (6:20 Beth-shemesh). Prophetic word shapes history; not everything revealed. Jonathan, David, Abigail call on God’s power for Yahweh’s battles. Samuel and David frame the “dark, problematical figure of King Saul”; all three forerunners of “the real King.” In Saul and David one may see God’s “justice” and “mercy,” fulfilled in NT in Christ. Messianic promise deferred to 2 Samuel volume Introduction.
- **Quote:** "in God’s dealings with Saul and David, one might see God’s “justice” and his “mercy,” respectively; both aspects will be fulfilled, according to the NT, in the person of Jesus Christ"
- **Locus:** [Pages 71–73]; §IX.C God’s Sovereign Will and Power
- **Targets:** [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[david]], [[jonathan]], [[divine-providence]], [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-45 | Purpose of 1 Samuel: monarchy + David’s preparation; prophet over king; messianic obedience note
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Purpose of 1 Samuel: highlight (1) establishment of monarchy in Israel (chs. 8–12) and (2) preparation of David to sit on throne after Saul (chs. 16–31). Saul ruled only “two years” (on 13:1) in God’s eye long rejected as Yahweh’s vice-regent (on 16:1), though humanly on throne till Gilboa. 2 Sam 7 will promise David eternal dynasty (“Davidic covenant” in vol. 2). Samuel as kingmaker anoints first Saul then David—setting principle that Israel’s king is subject to the prophet conveying God’s word; obedience to God’s word necessary condition for acceptable king. Jesus the Messiah-king embodied this obedience “even unto the death of the cross” (Phil 2:8).
- **Quote:** "1 Samuel sets the principle that the king in Israel is to be subject to the prophet through whom God conveys his word."
- **Locus:** [Page 73]; §X Purpose of 1 Samuel
- **Targets:** [[1-samuel]], [[2-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[saul]], [[david]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[monarchy-request]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[covenant]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

## Method claims

### M-R1-01 | Linguistic priority before history/theology
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Balanced exegesis requires understanding linguistic aspects as much as possible before reconstructing history or theology.
- **Quote:** "the linguistic aspects of the relevant text need to be understood as much as possible before attempting to reconstruct the history or theology."
- **Locus:** [Page 46]; §V Grammar and Syntax
- **Targets:** [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]], [[1-samuel]]

### M-R1-02 | Prefer phonological/grammatical explanation over emendation
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Seek phonological, grammatical, idiomatic (brachylogy), and aural explanations of unusual forms before orthographic/text-critical solutions; leave MT unaltered when evidence of corruption is insufficient.
- **Quote:** "When there is not enough evidence to draw the solid conclusion that the text is corrupt, the best thing to do is to leave the MT, an ancient artifact, unaltered"
- **Locus:** [Page 10]; §II.B.5
- **Targets:** [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### M-R1-03 | Discourse grammar as distinctive commentary method
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Applies foreground/background, Longacre verb-rank, SETTING–EVENT–TERMINUS, Parunak links, tempo, and viewpoint analysis thoroughly to Samuel—claimed as first such commentary.
- **Quote:** "no commentary has appeared which applies this analysis thoroughly to the Hebrew text of 1–2 Samuel."
- **Locus:** [Page 50]; §VI intro
- **Targets:** [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]], [[1-samuel]]

### M-R1-04 | Comparative-contextual maximalism
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Use comparison and contrast within entire Near Eastern context; archaeology illuminates/illustrates; absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence; use every scrap of evidence (Hallo maximalist vs Thompson/Davies minimalist).
- **Quote:** "we should make full use of these precious pieces of evidence from the ancient Near East, not so much to prove that the Bible is true but to illuminate and illustrate"
- **Locus:** [Pages 27–28]; §III.C.2
- **Targets:** [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### M-R1-05 | Vertical grammar + AXB + poetic prose as exegetical tools
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Analyze narrative as aural/poetic with vertical grammar and AXB insertion; many “corrupt” or conflate readings (McCarter et al.) dissolve under these tools.
- **Quote:** "recognizing this technique can solve many cruces interpretum in Samuel."
- **Locus:** [Page 61]; §VII.C
- **Targets:** [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]], [[1-samuel]]

### M-R1-06 | Synchronic reading with historical competence
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Final-form literary reading has priority over diachronic source dissection for understanding the text as it stands, but full understanding requires historical knowledge of languages, conventions, genres, and ANE settings—not free-floating reader-response/deconstruction.
- **Quote:** "we cannot fully understand a text unless we know the starting point for the authors and redactors, their languages, conventions, and genres"
- **Locus:** [Page 20]; §III.B.2
- **Targets:** [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

## Structure/theology summary

**Literary architecture (Tsumura):**
1. **Story of Samuel** (1 Sam 1:1–7:17) with embedded Ark Narrative (4:1–7:1)
2. **Transition to monarchy** (ch. 8: “Appoint us a king”)
3. **Story of Saul** (9:1–15:35)
4. **Story of Saul and David** (16:1–31:13)
5. **Story of King David** (2 Sam 1–20), linked by 2 Sam 1 as A/aB hinge
6. **Epilogues** (2 Sam 21–24), concentric ABCBA, not secondary appendices

**Poetic frame:** Hannah’s Song (1 Sam 2) + David’s Song/Last Words (2 Sam 22–23) form inclusio for whole 1–2 Samuel; 2 Sam 1 elegy opens second book parallel to Hannah’s narrative-then-poem opening.

**Hannah’s Song themes:** (1) Yahweh’s holy sovereignty; (2) reversal of human fortunes; (3) kingship—load-bearing program for the books.

**Theology (Tsumura):**
- Yahweh alone is eternal King; human king = vice-regent/deputy only ([[kingship-in-israel]], [[monarchy-request]]).
- Providential guidance of ordinary life ([[divine-providence]]); not Fate.
- Davidic covenant (2 Sam 7) as turning point toward Messianic line ([[davidic-covenant]])—full treatment deferred to vol. 2.
- Obedience to prophetic word as criterion of acceptable kingship; justice (Saul) / mercy (David) pointing to Christ.

**Purpose (explicit):** Establish monarchy (8–12) + prepare David for throne (16–31); prophet-over-king principle; messianic obedience of Jesus as fulfillment note.

## Date/authorship/DH position

**Authorship:** Unknown; “Samuel” = key figure/king-maker, not author (dies mid-book).

**Tsumura’s compositional sketch (tentative, attributed):**
| Unit | Suggested setting |
|---|---|
| Ark (1 Sam 4:1–7:1) | Possibly pre-Davidic / contemporary with Samuel |
| Story of Samuel (1–7) + ch. 8 “Right of the King” | Early Samuel ministry |
| Story of Saul (9–15) | Later Samuel era |
| Story of Saul and David (16–31) | Early David (justify vs Saulides) |
| Story of King David (2 Sam 1–20) | Late David / early Solomon |
| Epilogues (2 Sam 21–24) | United Monarchy material, integral to final whole |
| **Final edit** | **≤ late 10th c. B.C., early Rehoboam** (1 Sam 27:6 Ziklag) |

**On putative sources:** AN, HDR, SN/CH widely posited; Tsumura doubts they existed as independent single works; prefers his story-unit labels and unified final narrative about establishing David’s throne.

**On Deuteronomistic History:** Skeptical of Noth/Cross-style late Dtr redaction for Samuel based on “Deuteronomistic language.” Argues circularity; ANE and early-biblical parallels for key phrases; archaic vocabulary retained; early historiography possible (Gordon, Millard, Laato on eternal dynasty). Final editors did minimal framing (citing Alter), not major exilic rewrite. **Remains hypothetical.**

**Historicity stance:** Maximalist-leaning (Hallo); Tel Dan *bytdwd* etc. support David’s historicity against minimalists.
